newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Fed's Truman voices concerns about EMU.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Fed's Truman voices concerns about EMU.

text.p: A senior Federal Reserve official voiced wide-ranging concerns about European monetary union and said it could lead to a "step backward" in economic policy coordination among nations.

Speaking at a conference sponsored by the International Monetary Fund, Fed Staff Director Edwin Truman also warned Europe against expecting any big financial bonus from the launch of the euro and said that any erosion of the dollar's role as the world's key currency after 1999 would be gradual.

"I'm a bit concerned that too much thinking about coordination of policy within Europe appears to be focussed on something called exchange rate policy rather than on more serious issues of of fundamental economic policy," Truman, who is the U.S. central bank's top international bureaucrat, said.
Such a shift in focus, the Fed official said, would be a "step backward" because it would distract attention from fiscal and monetary policy.
Rather than seeing currency rates as a "performance variable" that results from the mix of macroeconomic policies, it would mean setting them up as a policy objective, he said.

Truman noted that many Europeans seem to be hoping that the introduction of the euro on Jan. 1, 1999 will end the dollar's hegemony as the world's key reserve currency, bringing Europe big financial benefits in the process.
"My concern is that this line of thinking is seriously misguided," he said, adding, "There is a big risk that this might be one more disappointment of EMU."

Truman, who emphasized that he was speaking for himself at the conference and not the Fed, said that Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) could make economic policy coordination more difficult both internationally and within Europe itself.

He voiced scepticism that Europe's proposed Stablity Council would prove adequate to ensuring smooth coordination between the new regional central bank and the individual member nations that make up EMU and their budget policies.
Truman also questioned whether Europe would have sufficient mechanisms in place to ensure financial stability in the banking system and elsewhere.
"That may be more of a problem down the road than some people care to admit," he said.
With the coordination of fiscal and monetary policy potentially so complicated, Truman saw a risk that Europe would focus on other areas, such as foreign exchange rates.

"One of the concerns ... is that the world will take a step backward in fact to a world in which the focus will be on exchange rates rather than on the underlying economic and financial policies, including fiscal and monetary policies," he said.
Truman though doubted that the advent of EMU would lead to a global system of fixed exchange rates or currency target zones. "That is quite frankly unlikely," he said.
Truman though did express concern that EMU might make it more difficult for the IMF to cope with future Mexico-style crises that threaten the international monetary system.

That could occur because Europe might be so preoccupied with its own problems that it would fail to appreciate the risks of such a crisis to the system as a whole, and thus prevent the IMF from using its emergency resources to cope.
"Europe could do some real damage, not just because it might not reach the right decision," Truman said. "It might not be able to reach any decision in time."
